source.title: Next-token pretraining implies in-context learning
source.authors: P. Riechers; Henry R. Bigelow; Eric A. Alt; A. Shai

record.tranche_reason: The paper reports results on in-context loss as context position changes, including a power law in that variable. It does not test loss scaling with model parameters, training tokens, or compute, nor compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper studies synthetic-process in-context loss as a function of context position. Those results are related to loss power laws but do not measure the scaling variables named by V1–V7. It cites Kaplan et al. [25] but does not test their scaling laws. No rows are included for the induction-head phase transition or other training-loss dynamics because they do not bear on the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study measures in-context loss as a function of context position on synthetic processes. It does not vary parameters, training tokens or compute, and it does not measure compute-optimal allocation, architecture shape at fixed size, or downstream tasks. It cites Kaplan et al. Fig. 20 only as motivation, saying power-law in-context loss was observed there. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors argue that in-distribution in-context learning necessarily follows from minimising next-token loss, and that non-ergodic or context-free structure yields power-law in-context loss. They also claim in-context performance on a task is coupled to the ensemble of tasks seen in pretraining. They make no claim about parameter, data or compute scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses information-theoretic analysis and synthetic correlated-token processes to study context-position loss; it does not reproduce the original parameter/token/compute scaling experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported in-context loss depends on context position and data-process structure; the power-law behavior is described for large numbers of ergodic components or for context-free/context-sensitive correlations. The paper also reports that a BOS token is important for fitting the first few context positions in some experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: On a uniform mixture of N biased coins as N grows large, excess myopic entropy decays about as 1/2 times ℓ^-1 in context position. Transformer log-log curves become linear for large N.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In-context loss follows a power law in context position when the training data are non-ergodic (many latent components) or context-free.

fits_no_version.finding: Transformers' in-context loss converges during training to the theoretical myopic entropy curve set by the data's correlational structure. IID data shows no reduction with context.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The in-context loss profile is determined by the data process's predictive-state metadynamic.

record.problems: The experiments use synthetic processes and small models, so they do not establish the listed scaling laws for language-model parameter count, training tokens, or compute. Experimental values are mainly presented in figures; no model-size scaling sweep is reported.
record.rows_left_out: No results measuring model-parameter, training-token, or compute scaling were reported. Other process-specific context-loss curves in Figure 1 and Figure 2 were omitted where they did not report the power-law/context-loss findings captured above. Training-loss phase-transition and induction-head results were omitted as they do not bear on the listed versions.

untested.parts: No sweep of parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small runs to large runs.
No shape variation at fixed parameter count. The paper only remarks that architectural details were not critical once a BOS token was used.
The power law is in context position on synthetic data, not in training scale.

record.verdict_notes: The record's gating is correct. The power law here is in context position, which is a different construct from the claim's training-scale laws, so it belongs under fits_no_version.

versions.untested_parts: Does not sweep parameter count, training tokens, or training compute to measure held-out pretraining loss.
Does not fit scaling laws on small runs and evaluate predictions on larger runs.
Does not compare parameter/token allocations at fixed compute or estimate their growth with compute.
Does not vary depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
Synthetic token processes are studied, but the paper does not test whether the specified parameter/token/compute power law holds across modalities or the listed training regimes.
Does not measure downstream task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitting choices or setups for the parameter/token/compute scaling laws or compute-optimal split.
